A New Theory for Prison Reform The Stanford Prison Experiment might have become a forgotten footnote in the history of psychology if not for what happened next. The day after the experiment ended abruptly on August 20, 1971, there was an attempted prison break at San Quentin Penitentiary, just 90 minutes north of Stanford. Three inmates and three guards were killed in the melee. Just weeks later, rioting inmates overpowered guards at the Attica Correctional Facility in New York; 43 people, including 10 hostages, were killed during the ensuing uprising and retaking of the prison. The outcome was shocking. Students taking part in the Stanford Prison Experiment in August 1971. It started with a classified ad in the “help wanted” section of the Palo Alto Times. Between job postings for Avon reps and security system sales was an ad reading: “Male College students needed for psychological study of prison life. $15 per day for 1-2 weeks beginning Aug. 15. The previous semester, some of Zimbardo’s undergraduate students had built a small mock prison in their dorm for a class project studying the psychological effects of incarceration on both prisoners and guards. The results were alarming. Over just three days, the role-playing prisoners became despondent and desperate, and the guards turned into bullies. Zimbardo was intrigued. He had become too immersed in his dual role as the principal investigator and the prison superintendent, and overlooked the escalating abuse and distress among participants. It was only after an external observer, Christina Maslach, raised concerns about the participants’ well-being that Zimbardo terminated the study. Zimbardo aimed to study situational forces versus disposition. He wanted to see how people would conform to the roles of prisoner or guard in a simulated prison environment. He wanted to explore why prison behavior occurs. Was it due to the inherent personalities of prisoners and guards, or the prison’s own social structure and environment? What were the results of the Stanford Prison Experiment? The results of the Stanford Prison Experiment showed that situational factors and power dynamics played a significant role in shaping participants’ behavior. The guards became abusive and authoritarian, while the prisoners became submissive and emotionally distressed. The experiment revealed how quickly ordinary individuals could adopt and internalize harmful behaviors due to their assigned roles and the environment. Who Was Philip Zimbardo? Philip Zimbardo (1933–2024) was an American social psychologist who spent most of his career at Stanford University. He grew up in poverty in the South Bronx. A Landmark, Controversial Study On Sunday, August 14, real Palo Alto police officers arrived at the dorms and homes of the prisoners with sirens blaring. They cuffed the prisoners, read them their Miranda rights and booked them at the station on charges of burglary and armed robbery. Then, blindfolded, the students were taken to “prison,” three mocked-up cells in the basement of Jordan Hall on the Stanford campus. What happened in that fake prison over the next six days is the stuff of legend. The Stanford Prison Experiment was supposed to run for two weeks, but Zimbardo had to call it off early when things spiraled out of control.

passages.text: Stanford prison experiment | Stanford prison experiment | | |---|---| | Date | August 14–21, 1971 | |---|---| | Location | | | Also known as | Zimbardo prison experiment SPE ZPE | | Type | Psychological experiment | The Stanford prison experiment (SPE) was a controversial psychological experiment performed in August 1971 at Stanford University. It was designed to be a two-week simulation of a prison environment that examined the effects of situational variables on participants' reactions and behaviors. Stanford psychology professor Philip Zimbardo managed the research team that administered the study.[1] Participants were recruited from the local community through an advertisement in the newspapers offering US$15 (equivalent to $119.25 in 2025) per day to male college students who agreed to participate in a "psychological study of prison life". Twenty-four participants were chosen after assessments of psychological stability and then assigned randomly to the role of prisoners or prison guards.[2] Critics have questioned the validity of these methods.[3] Those volunteers selected to be "guards" were given uniforms designed specifically to de-individuate them, and they were instructed to prevent prisoners from escaping. The experiment started officially when "prisoners" were arrested by the real police of Palo Alto, California. During the

Prisoners had full mental breakdowns. Even Zimbardo, acting as the prison’s “superintendent,” later said he got swept up in his role and nearly forgot it was all fake. More than 50 years later, the Stanford Prison Experiment remains one of the most famous psychological studies in the history of the field. Its shocking conclusion, that “ordinary college students could do terrible things,” has been used to explain prison riots and abuses at the Abu Ghraib prison in Iraq. But the Stanford Prison Experiment is also hugely controversial. Not only would its methods be considered dangerously unethical by today’s standards, but its key findings have also been called into question. After one of the prisoners (No. 8612) was released, the guards heard a rumor that he and some friends were going to return that night and attempt a prison break. As superintendent, Zimbardo was prepared to take extreme measures to protect his prison. Zimbardo asked the Palo Alto Police Department if he could transfer his prisoners to the department’s old jail. When the police refused, Zimbardo was “angry and disgusted at this lack of cooperation between our correctional facilities.” Zimbardo considered chaining the prisoners together, putting bags over their heads and taking them to a fifth-floor storage room until the threat of a prison break had passed.
